strengths: Strong theoretical foundation: The paper provides a rigorous derivation of closed-form optimal blockwise transforms for joint weight-activation quantization under both integer and floating-point formats, providing clear mathematical insights into why previous orthogonal transforms are suboptimal.

Data-aware and closed-form: Unlike prior learned rotation methods (e.g., SpinQuant) that require expensive optimization, WUSH computes the optimal transforms analytically using second-order statistics in a single calibration pass.

Convincing empirical performance: Significant accuracy improvements are shown across several LLMs (Llama-3.2, Llama-3.1, Qwen3) for modern low-bit formats such as MXFP4, NVFP4, and INT4, outperforming standard RTN and Hadamard transforms.
weaknesses: Lack of hardware/latency evaluation: Since WUSH applies a unique transform per block, it lacks the hardware-friendly uniformity of Hadamard rotations. The paper does not provide actual inference latency or throughput benchmarks to evaluate the practical system overhead.

Limited evaluation setting: The method is only integrated and evaluated with basic Round-To-Nearest (RTN) quantization. Its compatibility and performance when combined with more advanced PTQ methods (e.g., GPTQ) are left to future work.

Calibration overhead details: Although the method is closed-form, it requires computing Cholesky and eigenvalue decompositions for every block in all layers. The paper lacks details or quantitative analysis of the wall-clock time required for this calibration process.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and important problem in LLM quantization: explaining and improving upon the empirically successful but data-agnostic blockwise transforms (like the Hadamard transform) using data-aware statistics.

The theoretical framework is mathematically rigorous and clean. The authors succeed in deriving closed-form optimal transforms (WUSH) for joint weight-activation quantization for both floating-point (FP) and integer (INT) formats under a probabilistic framework.
The paper explains why the Hadamard transform is highly effective as a data-agnostic component, showing that it naturally emerges as the optimal backbone of the data-aware formulation.

The evaluation covers several recent, widely-used LLMs (Llama-3, Qwen-3) and evaluates modern micro-scaling formats like MXFP4 and NVFP4, showing solid improvements in perplexity/accuracy over standard RTN and Hadamard baselines.
weaknesses: The practical inference overhead of WUSH is a major concern. Unlike blockwise Hadamard transforms, which are orthogonal and can be computed very efficiently in $O(d \log d)$ time with a single shared matrix across all blocks, WUSH assigns a distinct, non-orthogonal transform matrix $T_{hsvx(i)}$ to each individual block $i$. Performing a unique general matrix-vector multiplication for every block of activations online during inference will introduce significant latency overhead, likely eclipsing any speedup gained from 4-bit quantization. The paper lacks actual hardware latency or throughput measurements to show if this method is practical.

The paper lacks experimental comparisons with state-of-the-art rotation-based post-training quantization methods, such as SpinQuant or FlatQuant, which also utilize calibration data to optimize transforms. Even though WUSH has the advantage of being closed-form and training-free, comparing accuracy and search/calibration time against these methods is necessary to contextualize the performance gains.

The analysis assumes an unbiased stochastic quantizer with independent round-to-nearest noise to make the derivation tractable. In practice, LLM quantizers are deterministic (nearest rounding), and activation distributions have highly structured outlier channels rather than being fully independent. This gap between the theoretical assumptions and real-world distributions is not fully characterized.

Details regarding reproducibility are somewhat scarce, particularly concerning how the simulation of the emerging hardware formats (like NVFP4 and MXFP4) was set up, and whether the code will be made open-source to facilitate further research.

strengths: Elegant and rigorous theoretical derivation: The paper provides the first closed-form optimal linear blockwise transforms for joint weight-activation quantization, linking data-dependent statistics with the Hadamard transform backbone.

Addresses highly relevant formats: The work analyzes and derives optimal transforms for both floating-point (MXFP4, NVFP4) and integer (INT4) block-quantized formats, which are key to modern hardware architectures.
Calibration-free and closed-form: Unlike optimization-based rotation methods (such as SpinQuant), WUSH computes the transforms analytically from calibration data, avoiding expensive training.

Strong empirical validation: Experiments on multiple LLM families (Llama-3.2, Llama-3.1, Qwen3) across diverse downstream tasks demonstrate consistent accuracy improvements over both standard RTN and baseline Hadamard transforms.
weaknesses: Inference overhead and practical system feasibility: Unlike the Hadamard transform, which is orthogonal and can be applied globally using the fast Walsh-Hadamard transform (FWHT), WUSH uses block-specific, non-orthogonal transforms. Multiplying activations by unique $d \times d$ matrices per block at inference time introduces noticeable computational and memory overhead. The paper lacks hardware benchmark results or wall-clock speedups to show if the accuracy gains outweigh the runtime costs.

Theoretical-practical gap in quantization modeling: The theoretical derivation relies on the assumption of a stochastic, unbiased quantizer (Section 2.1) and smooth approximation models. In practice, LLM quantization commonly uses deterministic Round-to-Nearest (RTN) with AbsMax scaling, which introduces some discrepancy between the theoretically proven optimality and the actual implementation.

Baselines in experiments: The comparison is primarily against Identity and Hadamard transforms. Comparing against other post-training outlier-mitigation or transformation methods (such as AWQ, SmoothQuant, or SpinQuant) would provide a more complete picture of WUSH's performance trade-offs.

strengths: Rigorous Theoretical Derivation: The paper provides a solid theoretical foundation, deriving closed-form optimal blockwise transforms for both floating-point and integer quantization formats. This beautifully explains the empirical success of the Hadamard transform and extends it to data-dependent scenarios.

Practical GPU Implementation: A key challenge of per-block adaptive transforms is the online inference overhead. The authors address this by implementing a highly optimized fused GPU kernel using CUTLASS, achieving speedups of up to 6.6x over BF16 with only a 1.3% overhead compared to data-agnostic transforms.

Significant Accuracy Improvements: WUSH shows strong empirical gains over state-of-the-art baselines (like MR-GPTQ and SpinQuant) across multiple LLM families (Llama-3, Qwen-3) under 4-bit weight-activation quantization (MXFP4, NVFP4, and INT4).

Excellent Intuitive Visualizations: The manuscript provides outstanding 2D visualizations (e.g., Figures 1 and 4) that make the complex geometrical effects of the transforms highly intuitive and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Computational Overhead of Offline Calibration: The offline calibration phase (Algorithm 1) involves computing SVDs and Cholesky decompositions block-by-block, interleaved with GPTQ. The manuscript would benefit from a quantitative breakdown of the calibration time compared to standard GPTQ or SpinQuant.

Evaluation Limited to 4-bit Quantization: The empirical evaluation focuses predominantly on W4A4 (MXFP4/NVFP4/INT4) settings. Showing results on lower bitwidths (such as W2 or W3) or different activation-group configurations would further demonstrate the generalization of the theory.

strengths: Strong Theoretical Foundation: The paper provides a rigorous mathematical derivation of optimal closed-form blockwise transforms for weight-activation quantization. It covers both integer (INT) and floating-point (FP) formats, and offers a clear explanation of why data-agnostic Hadamard rotations have historically been so effective.

Data-Aware and Efficient: Unlike prior data-aware transform methods (such as SpinQuant or FlatQuant) that rely on computationally expensive training or fine-tuning, WUSH is purely calibration-based and calculated in closed form using second-order statistics.

Hardware-level Practicality: The authors do not just rely on simulated results; they provide a fused GPU kernel implemented in CUTLASS. It addresses the challenges of using a unique transform per block, achieving up to 6.6x speedup over BF16 on modern hardware with negligible overhead compared to fixed Hadamard transforms.

Comprehensive Evaluation: WUSH is validated extensively across multiple state-of-the-art LLM families (Llama-3, Qwen3) ranging from 3B to 70B parameters, demonstrating major improvements in accuracy (especially for W4A4 in MXFP4 and NVFP4 formats) compared to strong baselines.
weaknesses: Discussion on Calibration Overhead: While WUSH is closed-form, performing Cholesky and SVD decompositions for every block across all layers of a massive model (like a 70B parameter model) still incurs some overhead. The manuscript would be improved by reporting the actual wall-clock calibration time compared to standard GPTQ or Hadamard baselines.

Assumptions and Simplifications: The theoretical proof relies on several simplifying assumptions, such as treating quantization errors as stochastic/unbiased and approximating the FP casting error via a smoothed SEaMb format. Although these are standard and empirically validated here, a brief qualitative discussion on scenarios where these assumptions might degrade would add valuable depth.

strengths: Strong Theoretical Contribution: The paper provides the first closed-form derivation of optimal, non-orthogonal blockwise transforms for both floating-point (FP) and integer (INT) block quantizers. It elegantly explains the empirical success of Hadamard rotations (as the sole data-agnostic component) and demonstrates how incorporating second-moment data-dependent statistics yields near-optimal performance.

Excellent GPU Kernel Support: A common pitfall of block-specialized adaptive transforms is the high overhead of online inference. The authors address this by implementing a highly optimized fused CUTLASS GEMM-equivalent kernel. The implementation achieves up to 6.63× speedup over BF16 on Blackwell hardware (RTX 5090) and incurs only an average 1.3% throughput difference compared to data-agnostic blockwise Hadamard.

Comprehensive Empirical Evaluation: WUSH is validated across multiple state-of-the-art LLMs (Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B/14B/32B) using challenging low-bit micro-scaling formats (MXFP4, NVFP4, and INT4), showing significant accuracy improvements.

Clear Exposition and Intuitive Visualizations: The 2D illustration in Figure 1 and the discussion on multivariate vs. univariate probabilistic modeling (Section A.2) do an outstanding job of clarifying how WUSH shapes the quantization noise.
weaknesses: Notation Inconsistencies and Typos: There is some confusion regarding the assignment of the weight transform ($T_{wush}$) versus the activation transform ($T_{xvsh}$). In Equation 10, the forward pass applies $T_{wush(i)}$ to the activations $\tilde{X}_{(i)}$, whereas Equation 8 defines $T_{xvsh(i)}$ as the activation transform and $T_{wush(i)}$ as the weight transform. In Algorithm 1 Line 8, the computed expression actually corresponds to $T_{xvsh(i)}$ but is assigned to `Twush(i)`. These naming discrepancies should be aligned to ensure readability.

Interleaved GPTQ Complexity: The integration of WUSH with GPTQ requires an interleaved computational schedule (Algorithm 1) to handle the mutual dependence between weight updates and transform statistics. This adds non-trivial complexity to the offline calibration pipeline.
